question: In its decision on a complaint submitted by the European Organisation of Military Associations and Trade Unions, the European Committee of Social Rights (ESCR) found the Irish Government to be in breach of the European Social Charter with regard to the working conditions of members of the Irish Defence Forces.

Indeed, the ECSR found Ireland to be in violation of Article 2(2) of the Charter with regard to Defence Forces members who perform duties on public holidays and who do not receive allowances linked to specific functions.

Ireland is also in violation of Article 4(2) of the Charter as a result of the absence of adequate arrangements for the compensation of overtime, compounded by both the lack of a time and attendance registration system and the exclusion of overtime discussions from the conciliation and arbitration framework.
This ruling may also have relevance to the Directive 2003/88/EC and to Article 31 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union. Given the ruling: 1.
Does the Commission believe that all EU Member States signed up to the Social Charter should fulfil their obligations to it?
Could the Commission outline any communication it has had with the Irish authorities since the publication of the ruling?
Could the Commission confirm whether it believes that the Irish authorities must commit themselves to addressing the violations so that members of the Irish Defence Forces enjoy their full rights?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.7.2026) The European Social Charter is a treaty of the Council of Europe1. The obligations under this treaty are a matter for the Council of Europe to examine. The national Working Time Act2, that implements Directive 2003/88/EC,3 applies to the Defence forces in this case and this is not contested (point 83 of the decision).

The Directive does not regulate the issue of remuneration for work performed during public holidays, nor is there any other EU law specifically governing pay for overtime hours. The Directive does not make separate provisions for overtime, which is counted as working time.

Member States must require employers to set up, at a reasonable cost, an objective, reliable and accessible system enabling the duration of time worked by worker to be measured, in order to ensure the effectiveness of the Directive4. It is for the competent national authorities, to ensure that national rules, including those transposing Directive 2003/88/EC, are correctly and effectively applied.
1 https://rm.coe.int/168007cf93. 2 S.I. No. 11/2025 – European Communities (Organisation of Working Time) (Defence Forces) Regulations

2025 of 20 January 2025. 3 Directive 2003/88/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 November 2003 concerning certain aspects of the organisation of working time, OJ L 299, 18.11.2003, p. 9–19 - https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/88/oj/eng. 4 Judgment of 14 May 2019, Federación de Servicios de Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) v Deutsche Bank SAE, C-55/18, ECLI:EU:C:2019:402.
